instruction: What does $? contain after a function finishes running?
response: It holds the exit status of the last command that executed inside the function, which is the closest thing Bash has to a function return value. After a pipeline, $? likewise reports the status of the final command in the pipe.

instruction: What does DNS mean by a zone, and how is it different from a domain?
response: A domain such as groucho.edu covers every host beneath that name, while the zone holds only the hosts that the zone's own administrators manage directly. If physics.groucho.edu has been delegated to someone else, those machines belong to a separate zone even though they are still inside the domain.

instruction: I set up eth0 with ifconfig on a class B network that I split into class C subnets. What netmask do I pass and what goes wrong if I skip it?
response: Pass the subnet mask explicitly, for example `ifconfig eth0 vstout netmask 255.255.255.0`. Without it ifconfig guesses the mask from the address class and ends up with 255.255.0.0, which is wrong for the class C subnet.

instruction: I need the format of a config file in the man pages; which section do I use and where are the pages stored?
response: File formats are documented in section 5 of the manual, so look in man5. All the manual pages sit under /usr/share/man, split into eight numbered sections, with section 8 reserved for administration programs.

instruction: Where can I install a program I compiled myself so a system upgrade won't overwrite it?
response: Put it under /usr/local, which mirrors the layout of /usr and is kept safe from being overwritten when the distribution updates its own software. Admin tools you built yourself belong in /usr/local/sbin rather than mixed into the system directories.

instruction: My script is misbehaving and I can't tell why. How can I watch every command as bash runs it?
response: Start the script with bash -x script.sh, or put the option on the first line, like #!/bin/bash -xv. Each command is printed with a leading + after expansion but before it executes, so you can see exactly which values were substituted.

instruction: Should I use [ ] or [[ ]] for tests in a script, and how do they differ?
response: The single bracket is a builtin that is just another name for the test command, so Bash treats what is inside as ordinary arguments. The double bracket arrived in Bash 2.02 as an extended test and is a keyword, so the shell parses the whole expression as one unit and comparisons feel more like other programming languages.

instruction: Swap partition or swap file: which one should I pick?
response: A swap partition is faster, but a swap file is easier to resize because you don't have to repartition the disk. If you already know how much swap you need, go with a partition; if not, start with a file, watch real usage for a while, and switch to a partition once the size is settled.

instruction: Is the kernel the same thing as the operating system?
response: No. The kernel is only the core that tracks files, schedules programs, hands out memory and moves network packets, while a complete operating system also includes system programs such as mount, plus compilers, libraries and documentation that run on top of it in user mode.

instruction: How do X.25 and Frame Relay differ, and what do they have in common when it comes to hardware?
response: Frame Relay has quite a few technical traits in common with X.25 but behaves much more like IP, so it suits carrying TCP/IP between sites. Both need special synchronous serial hardware, which is why many cards support both, or you can use an external box instead, a PAD for X.25 and a FRAD for Frame Relay.

instruction: Is there a limit on swap space size, and how many areas can I enable?
response: Each swap area is capped at 2 GB by the Linux memory manager, but you can run up to eight of them at the same time, which adds up to 16 GB in total. Bigger needs therefore have to be spread over several partitions or files.

instruction: How many file descriptors does every script start with, and which are they?
response: Three are open from the start: stdin is descriptor 0, stdout is 1 and stderr is 2. Descriptors 3 through 9 stay free, so you can open extra files or keep temporary copies of the standard streams for later restoring.

instruction: Why does typing in vim sometimes run commands instead of putting text in my file?
response: vi works in two modes, command mode and insert mode, and it always launches in command mode, so your keystrokes are treated as commands. Press i, a or o to start inserting text, and hit Esc whenever you want to get back to command mode.

instruction: Give me the tar commands to back up a directory, check the archive, and pull back one file.
response: Make the backup with `tar --create --file DEVICE /dir`, verify it afterwards using `tar --compare --verbose --file DEVICE`, and restore a single file with `tar xpvf DEVICE` followed by that file's path exactly as tar stored it, without the leading slash.

instruction: How long does a caching name server hold on to an answer it looked up?
response: Only until the record's time to live (TTL) runs out. The administrators of the zone that owns the data choose that value, and until it expires the local server can skip the walk down from the root and query the right server straight away.

instruction: When would plain chroot be enough, and when do I want QEMU with KVM instead?
response: A chroot is the lightest option and is fine for compiling programs, running console applications and daemons in another Debian release. If you need a whole desktop or a different system, QEMU with KVM gives full hardware-assisted emulation, whereas pure QEMU on its own is very slow.

instruction: When would I pick locate over find to look for a file?
response: locate answers almost instantly and uses few resources because it searches a prebuilt index, but that database is only refreshed once a day and the tool is more limited. find scans the directories live and can test size, modification date and other properties, at the cost of a trickier syntax and more system load.

instruction: What separates /sbin from /usr/sbin?
response: /sbin keeps the administration binaries that are essential for booting, restoring and repairing the system, like fdisk, init and ifconfig. /usr/sbin holds the other admin tools, such as network daemons and useradd, which are not needed for recovery; neither is normally in a regular user's PATH.

instruction: What does echo sp{el,il,al}l print, and when does brace expansion happen?
response: It prints spell spill spall, because the prefix sp and the suffix l get wrapped around each comma-separated item in turn. Brace expansion runs before every other kind of expansion and is purely textual, and the braces must contain at least one unquoted comma to be expanded at all.

instruction: How can I run cd and a few commands inside my script without changing its current directory?
response: Put them in parentheses so they run in a subshell, for example (cd $home; less .bashrc). Directory changes and variable assignments made inside the subshell don't carry back to the parent, so there's no need to cd back afterwards.

instruction: Set up a Debian server so it boots to the text console and not the GUI, and switch to it right now too.
response: Make the change permanent with "systemctl set-default multi-user", which changes the default target used at boot. To move the running system over immediately without rebooting, use "systemctl isolate multi-user", which stops the units that only the graphical target needs.

instruction: What problems were Linux distributions causing that led to the FSSTND being written?
response: In the early-to-mid 90s every distributor picked their own layout, so it was impossible to share a /usr partition, unclear what separated /bin from /usr/bin, and diskless workstations could not be set up. The standard was meant to end that confusion about where files belong.

instruction: Compare /tmp with /var/tmp for temporary data.
response: /tmp is for short-lived files, is usually emptied at boot or shutdown, and programs must never count on its contents surviving between runs. /var/tmp is meant for temporary files that are large or must last longer than /tmp allows, though an admin may still purge very old ones.

instruction: Where do password hashes live when shadow passwords are turned on, and why does that help?
response: They are moved out of /etc/passwd into /etc/shadow, which only root is allowed to read. Since ordinary users can no longer grab the hashes, cracking the passwords becomes a lot harder.

instruction: Show how to add a route for the 172.16.1.0 subnet, and say why the -net flag matters.
response: Run `route add -net 172.16.1.0`, and the kernel picks eth0 because that interface's network part matches the destination. The flag is needed because route sees nonzero host bits under the class B default and would otherwise treat the address as a single host rather than a network.

instruction: A colleague just left the company. How should I remove their account cleanly?
response: Consider disabling the account first, then delete their files, mailbox, mail aliases, print jobs and cron or at jobs, and finally remove their lines from /etc/passwd and /etc/group, including every group they joined. Running `find / -user username` turns up stray files outside the home directory, though it is slow on big or network-mounted disks.

instruction: Why does if [ -f $FILENAME ] break on names with spaces, and how do I fix it?
response: When the variable is unquoted, a name containing spaces is split into several words, so the test sees multiple words instead of a single path. Wrapping $FILENAME in double quotes fixes it, or you can use the [[ ]] form in place of [ ].

instruction: How should I edit /etc/sudoers safely?
response: Open it with the visudo command while logged in as root instead of a normal editor on the file. The file decides which users may run which commands with root privileges through sudo, so a broken edit can lock you out of admin rights.

instruction: Why can Debian get away with a umask of 0002 for normal users?
response: Every new account on Debian gets its own private group with the same name, and that user is its only member. Because of that, letting the group have write permission doesn't expose files to anyone else, so you can enable it by adding "umask 002" to ~/.bashrc.

instruction: How can I keep an eye on a log file while new lines are being written to it?
response: Use tail -f with the name of the log file. It prints the last few lines and then keeps displaying new ones as the file grows, which is why administrators rely on it for following logs.

instruction: Show me a quick way to replace a regex match everywhere in a file, in place.
response: Use sed with the in-place flag, like "sed -i -e 's/FROM_REGEX/TO_TEXT/g' file". For several files at once, perl -i -p -e with the same substitution works, and giving it -i.bak instead of -i keeps a backup copy of each original in case the pattern goes wrong.

instruction: What does the very first character in an ls -l listing tell me about an entry?
response: It shows the kind of file: a dash means a regular file, d a directory, l a link, s a socket, p a named pipe, and b a block device. Ordinary users mostly deal with regular files, executables, directories and links.

instruction: Which is less painful to configure, sendmail or Exim, and what do you give up by choosing Exim?
response: Exim's config is laid out in a more orderly way and is easier to follow than sendmail's notoriously cryptic one. The price is that Exim lacks direct UUCP support and only deals with domain-style addresses, which most sites can live with, and the overall setup effort is roughly similar.

instruction: I need to put the user penguin into the group bird. How do I do it so it actually takes effect?
response: Run "sudo usermod -aG bird penguin", or "sudo adduser penguin bird" on a typical Debian install, or edit the group files with vigr. The new membership only applies after a fresh login session, and a full cold reboot followed by logging in is the most dependable way to get that.

instruction: Is there a debugger built into Bash?
response: No, Bash only ships a few bare-bones debugging aids, and its syntax errors are often cryptic. The line number in an error is where the interpreter finally noticed the problem rather than where you made the mistake, so a missing done shows up as an unexpected end of file.

instruction: Why do Linux installs usually split one disk into several partitions?
response: Splitting the disk keeps damage contained: if one partition is corrupted or fills up, the others will most likely keep working. A runaway script that fills a separate data partition, for instance, will not bring down the system partition.

instruction: Show how to send both stdout and stderr of a command into the same log file.
response: Append the file first and then duplicate stderr onto stdout, as in command >> command.log 2>&1, and in Bash 4 the shorthand &>filename does the same job. The order matters, since writing 2>&1 before the file redirect leaves the error message going to the terminal instead of the log.

instruction: Why did UNIX end up running on so many different kinds of hardware when earlier systems were tied to a single machine?
response: The Bell Labs team wrote UNIX in C instead of assembly and squeezed the machine-specific part down to a small kernel. Only that kernel had to be rewritten for each new computer, while everything built around it could be reused, which made porting far easier.

instruction: How does run level 1 differ from run levels 3 and 5?
response: Run level 1 is single-user mode where only the administrator can log in, which suits maintenance such as repairing disk corruption. Level 3 is full multiuser mode without a graphical session, and level 5 is the same with X11 so you get a graphical login.

instruction: My SSH link to a server drops a lot and I keep losing running jobs. Any way around that?
response: Start screen once you are logged in and run your programs inside its windows, opening new ones with ^A c. If the connection dies, or you detach on purpose with ^A d, log back in later and type "screen -r" to get all those windows and running programs back.

instruction: In tcpd, which file wins if a client matches entries in both hosts.allow and hosts.deny?
response: hosts.allow is checked first, so a match there grants access and hosts.deny is never looked at. A request that only matches hosts.deny gets its connection closed, and a request that matches neither file is simply let through.

instruction: How does a script hand back its exit status to the parent shell?
response: Use exit followed by an integer, and the parent receives that number in its $? variable. Zero means the script succeeded, while any other value can be picked freely by the author so the parent can react differently to each kind of failure, for example with a case statement.

instruction: Explain how to keep root from logging in over a modem or the network.
response: Edit /etc/securetty, which lists the terminals that root may log in from, and keep only the virtual consoles in it. Root logins from anywhere not listed are refused, which makes breaking in as superuser through a modem or network connection harder.

instruction: How far can I trust debsums when auditing a box for tampering?
response: Not very far. It compares installed files with MD5 sums kept locally under /var/lib/dpkg/info, and an intruder could alter those sums too. It is really only good for spotting changes an admin made by hand or damage caused by bad media.

instruction: Can a script start with a blank line before the shebang?
response: It shouldn't, because the file has to begin with the two characters #! and then the interpreter path. A blank line counts as a line of its own, so with one at the top the shebang would no longer be the first line.

instruction: I know a program lives in /opt/acroread/bin but the shell just says it can't find it. How do I get it to run?
response: Running which will confirm the directory is missing from your search path. You can either call the program with its full path, or append the directory to the variable with export PATH=$PATH:/opt/acroread/bin and then run it by name.

instruction: In awk, what do $0 and $1 refer to?
response: $0 holds the entire input line, while $1, $2 and so on hold the individual fields of that line. Fields are split on the field separator FS, which by default is one or more spaces or tabs.

instruction: I need some emergency swap fast on a running box. How do I set up a swap file?
response: Create a file without holes using dd from /dev/zero (choose a size that is a multiple of 4 KB), write the swap signature with mkswap, and then switch it on with swapon followed by the file path. If you want it used after every boot, add a line for it to /etc/fstab.

instruction: Show how to create a user account by hand without adduser or useradd.
response: Add a line to /etc/passwd using vipw with `*` in the password field, add a group through vigr if you need one, make the home directory and copy in the files from /etc/skel, then fix ownership and permissions with chown and chmod. Run passwd last, so the user cannot log in while things are half finished.

instruction: Which file does bash read when I open a terminal window from a menu icon rather than logging in?
response: A terminal opened from an icon or menu is an interactive non-login shell, so bash reads only ~/.bashrc. Login shells go through /etc/profile and then the first of ~/.bash_profile, ~/.bash_login or ~/.profile, which is why ~/.bash_profile often contains a line that sources ~/.bashrc.

instruction: Where does systemd pick up the machine's hostname at boot, and what belongs in that file?
response: The systemd-hostnamed.service unit reads /etc/hostname and hands the value to the kernel at boot. The file should hold just the short hostname on one line, not a fully qualified domain name.

instruction: How do I read the routing table to see where traffic for other networks is sent?
response: Run ip route show or the older netstat -nr. The line starting with 0.0.0.0 is the default route and names the gateway that receives traffic for hosts outside your network, whereas the line for your own subnet means packets just go out of the interface with no router involved.

instruction: How is an until loop different from a while loop?
response: Both repeat a block of commands based on the exit status of a test command, but a while loop keeps going as long as that test succeeds. An until loop does the opposite: it keeps going while the test fails and stops the moment it succeeds, though the syntax is otherwise identical.

instruction: Why does write-back caching make a sudden power cut riskier than write-through?
response: Write-through sends data to the disk immediately while keeping a cached copy, but write-back postpones the disk write to a later moment, which is faster. The catch is that a crash or power loss before the flush throws away pending changes and can leave the filesystem inconsistent, which is why you shut down properly or run sync.

instruction: Why do things like IRC DCC transfers break behind IP masquerade?
response: Masqueraded machines are invisible from the Internet, so services that depend on an outside host opening a connection back in have nothing to reach. Some protocols get around it with helper kernel modules that peek inside datagrams, but others have no support at all.

instruction: Give me a safer way to delete every .tmp file below the current directory without launching rm once per file.
response: First run find with -name "*.tmp" on its own to check that only the right files are selected. Then, instead of using -exec rm {} \; which starts rm for every single match, pipe the list into xargs rm so that rm is called only when the command line is full.

instruction: Fix the typo 'erors' and replace 'last' with 'final' in a text file using one sed command, keeping the result.
response: Chain two expressions with separate -e options: sed -e 's/erors/errors/g' -e 's/last/final/g' example. Since sed only writes to the terminal by default, add a redirect such as > fixed.txt to keep the result in a file.

instruction: exec versus just running a command in a script: what's the difference?
response: Normally the shell forks a child process to run the command and your script carries on afterwards. With exec no fork happens and the command replaces the shell itself, so once it finishes the script is finished too and any lines after it never run.

instruction: Ctrl+C and Ctrl+Z both stop a running program, so what separates them?
response: Ctrl+C sends SIGINT, the interrupt signal, to the job running in the foreground. Ctrl+Z sends SIGTSTP instead, which stops the program and hands control straight back to the shell, so one is an interrupt request and the other is a suspend.

instruction: How do hard links and symbolic links differ, and which of them can cross partitions?
response: A hard link is just a second name for the same inode and data blocks, and because inode numbers only make sense inside a single partition it can't reach across partitions. A symbolic link is a small file storing the path of its target, so it can point into another partition, though it breaks if the target is removed.

instruction: Should I let parted create and resize filesystems, or stick with mkfs and resize2fs?
response: Even though parted claims it can create and resize filesystems, the safer choice is the specialised, well-maintained tools such as mkfs.ext4 and resize2fs. Use parted mainly for the partition table itself, since it is gradually replacing fdisk for that job.

instruction: Older PCs versus UEFI machines: how does each one store the disk partition table?
response: Older PCs use the MBR scheme, which keeps the partition data in the very first sector (LBA 0, 512 bytes). UEFI machines use GPT, which does not keep it in that first sector. To convert a disk between them you wipe its first blocks and then run parted with mklabel gpt or mklabel msdos.

instruction: Should my PC's hardware clock run on local time or UTC?
response: UTC is usually the better choice, because then nothing has to be changed when daylight saving time starts or ends, and the kernel itself always keeps universal time anyway. Linux copes with either setting, but DOS, Windows and OS/2 expect local time, and a local-time hardware clock has to be adjusted by hand at each DST switch.

instruction: When would you choose dump over tar for backups?
response: dump reads the filesystem directly, so it leaves file timestamps alone, moves the disk heads less and has backup levels built in, which makes it better for full-filesystem backups. The price is that it only understands one filesystem type (ext2 on Linux), whereas tar works on any files and needs scripting to handle levels.

instruction: Why does Linux keep an ARP cache but still throw entries away after a while?
response: The cache saves the host from asking for the same Ethernet address on every datagram. Entries are dropped after some time because the remote machine's network card may have been swapped, which would leave a stale mapping behind, so a fresh query is forced.

instruction: Why does a Bash function that contains only comments throw a syntax error?
response: A function body can't be empty, and comment lines don't count as content, so the shell hits the closing brace and complains about an unexpected token. Putting a null command such as : inside the body is enough to make it valid.

instruction: When would I pick -eq over = in an if test?
response: Use -eq when comparing integers and = when comparing strings. They sometimes agree, but with a=273.0 the string test against 273 fails, and -eq against 273.0 aborts with an 'integer expression expected' error because that value isn't an integer.

instruction: A server is acting up and I don't know where to begin. Which directory has the logs, and how are they kept from ballooning?
response: Start in /var/log, which is a good first place to look for general problems, for example messages, syslog and auth.log. Since these files can grow without limit, logrotate normally runs from a daily cron job to rotate, compress, remove or mail them on a daily, weekly, monthly or size basis.

instruction: Which exit codes can a script hand back with the exit command?
response: exit takes an integer between 0 and 255. By convention 0 means the script succeeded and anything from 1 to 255 flags an error, and if you call exit with no argument the script just returns the status of the last command it ran.

instruction: The server feels sluggish and I can't tell why. Where should I start looking?
response: Work out which of the four usual bottlenecks is to blame: CPU, memory, disk I/O or network. Use top for a live view of load and per-process usage (press M to sort by memory, P by CPU), iostat for disk activity, and ps -ef for a full process listing.

instruction: Give me a quick way to print a multi-line message from a script without a pile of echo commands.
response: Use a here document with cat: write cat <<EndOfMessage, type the lines, and close with the same limit string alone on its own line. Switching to <<- strips leading tabs so the body can be indented, and variables inside the body still get expanded.

instruction: My ping to another machine on the same Ethernet gets no replies at all. Where should I start looking?
response: Check the packet counters shown by ifconfig to see whether anything left the interface, then log in to the other host and look at its counters too, so you can tell where the packets vanish. Also run `route -n` on both ends to confirm each has the right entry, and watch that the Use count rises between pings.

instruction: Compare where an input rule is applied in ipchains and in netfilter.
response: In ipfwadm and ipchains an input rule is checked as the datagram first arrives, before any routing decision. With netfilter the input rule moves to a later point, where only datagrams bound for the local machine pass, and the output rule likewise sits after local processes send, which changes how rulesets must be structured.

instruction: Show the right way to shut down a Linux machine and why just cutting power is risky.
response: Use shutdown, poweroff or init 0, or press ctrl-alt-del, so the partitions get unmounted properly. Linux holds a lot of disk writes in memory buffers, and unmounting flushes them; pulling the plug can leave important files in an undefined state.

instruction: Is ctime the moment a file was created?
response: No, ctime records when the file's status last changed, such as ownership or permission edits, while mtime tracks content modification and atime the last read. With the default relatime mount option, reading a file only refreshes atime the first time or if a day has passed.

instruction: How is /bin different from /usr/bin?
response: /bin holds the essential commands such as the shells, cp, mv, ls and mount, which must work even when only the root partition is mounted, for example when repairing other partitions in single user mode. /usr/bin holds the vast majority of other programs like vi and gcc, and /usr may live on a separate partition or even another machine.

instruction: Show how to switch tracing on for just one suspicious command inside a long script.
response: Put set -x on the line before the suspicious command and set +x right after it, so only that stretch gets traced. You can flip tracing on and off repeatedly inside the same script.
